description:
Solving SANS through a physical countermeasure system

I care about advancing civilization forward by expanding throughout the universe
summary: Spaceflight shifts about 2 litres of body fluid toward the head, and roughly 70% of astronauts on long ISS missions show signs of SANS (Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome): swollen optic nerves, flattened eyeballs and blurred vision. NASA ranks it among the top health risks to solve before Mars. We developed the SANS Prevention Project: a dynamic, pressure-controlled thigh cuff that senses the leg changing size as muscles tense and relax, and adjusts itself to hold a low venous pressure (about 40 mmHg). Today's cuffs, including NASA's flight cuff, are static, set to one tightness. We tested the idea in a pilot on a head-down tilt bed, an Earth model of the fluid shift. Without cuffs, eye pressure rose 4.6 mmHg. With cuffs it stayed near baseline, both lying still and during leg squeezes, at lower pressure than NASA-linked 60 mmHg cuffs. It is a one-participant pilot, honestly framed, with a clear path from idea to flight.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: A pair of upper-thigh cuffs applies low pressure (about 40 mmHg in our test; 25-35 mmHg planned) to hold some blood in the lower body, so less shifts toward the head in weightlessness. The proposed design uses a pressure sensor, a small controller and a pump/valve to vent when muscles tense and re-inflate when they relax, so it keeps working during a normal working day with no crew time.

HOW WE TESTED IT: One healthy participant lay on a hospital bed tilted 11.75° head-down (steeper than NASA's 6° bed-rest analog). Each run: 15 min flat, then 60 min tilted. Every 10 min we recorded eye pressure (iCare HOME2), blood pressure and heart rate (Beurer) and head fullness (0-10). Safety stop limits were set before the runs, and none was reached.

- Run 1, no cuffs: eye pressure +4.6 mmHg (peak +5.5), head fullness 1 to 4/10, visual distortions at 30 min.

- Run 2, cuffs, still: -0.7 mmHg, head fullness 1/10 throughout.

- Run 3, cuffs + leg squeezes every 5 min: +1.2 mmHg, head fullness 1/10 throughout.

10 of 12 Run 1 tilt readings were higher than all 24 cuffed readings. Compared with a NASA Johnson-linked study (60 mmHg set-pressure cuffs, -2.0 mmHg effect), our cuffs at 40 mmHg gave -5.3 mmHg at rest and -3.4 mmHg during squeezes.

IMPACT: SANS threatens astronaut vision and brain health on Moon and Mars missions, and there is no established treatment besides glasses and returning to Earth. A comfortable, self-adjusting, low-pressure cuff could protect crews during normal work, and could also help people on Earth with fluid-shift problems.

CREATIVITY: We target the gap in current cuffs (Braslet-M, NASA's laced flight cuff). They are static, and we hypothesize they loosen as the leg changes size. We apply proven self-regulating cuff technology from physiotherapy to a new problem, and we built a real experiment, including a new test of whether the cuff holds during muscle contraction.

VALIDITY AND HONESTY: This is a one-participant, unblinded pilot. Eye pressure, blood pressure and heart rate are indirect readings, not a SANS diagnosis. The cuffed changes are within our measurement spread (repeat readings differed by 2-5 mmHg). The loosening of static cuffs is a hypothesis we have not measured, and the NASA comparison is promising, not proof. We used commercial SAGA BFR Cuffs 2.0 as a stand-in for the purpose-built system. Our 6-step roadmap (engineering plan, funding, wearable build, independent validation with OCT/optic-nerve ultrasound and a fixed-cuff control, flight via Axiom or Voyager) is designed to close each gap.

RELEVANCE: The challenge asks for health monitoring that helps astronauts understand and act on their health. Our cuff is the "act" part and monitors itself as it works. Our study shows what to watch: eye pressure, blood pressure and heart rate that astronauts can self-measure.

TOOLS: SAGA BFR Cuffs 2.0, iCare HOME2 tonometer, Beurer BP monitor, Burmeier Dali tilt bed, UNI-T digital angle meter. Code-drawn charts and an interactive project page and slide deck. Claude (Anthropic) helped analyze data, write chart code and draft text. Our team ran every measurement, and nothing was simulated or AI-generated.

PRESENTATION: Project page and demo deck are linked below.
